Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Renata Okafor is a 37-year-old musician of mixed Nigerian-Canadian heritage who has lived in the United States for the past eleven years, building a modest but meaningful career as a session guitarist and occasional solo performer. She came to her first appointment carrying a guitar case she set down by the door and did not touch again for the entire session. She described herself, quietly, as someone who used to feel most alive on a stage and who now finds it difficult to sit in a room with more than four people without scanning every exit.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Renata was performing at an outdoor music festival in a mid-sized American city when a coordinated attack unfolded near the main stage. She had just finished a set and was standing at a merchandise table, still wearing her guitar strap, when the first explosion occurred roughly forty metres away. What followed was a period of chaos she described in fragmented but viscerally specific terms: the smell of smoke mixing with the food vendors' grease, the particular metallic taste that flooded her mouth as she dropped to the ground behind a equipment trunk, the sensation of the wooden stage planking vibrating beneath her palms, and the sound of the crowd shifting from applause to screaming in what felt like a single breath. She lay there for what she believes was around twenty minutes before emergency personnel reached her section. She was physically uninjured. Several people near her were not.

In the weeks that followed, Renata noticed that certain sensory details from that afternoon had not receded the way she expected them to. Her memories of the event remained extraordinarily clear and detailed — not softened by time but sharpened, as though each pass through them added resolution rather than distance. More distressing still, when the memories returned they did not feel like recollections. She would be in her kitchen and suddenly the metallic taste would be present in her mouth, unmistakable and unbidden, and with it the full weight of the ground beneath her, the vibration, the screaming — not as images recalled but as a reality momentarily reinstated. During these episodes she was not remembering the festival; she was, in some complete sensory sense, there again.

Renata works primarily in recording studios and small venues, environments that carry the ambient sounds and smells of live performance she once loved. Now, the particular combination of crowd noise bleeding through a studio monitor or the smell of stage equipment can interrupt a session entirely. She has begun arriving late to bookings to avoid the setup period when those cues are most concentrated, and has cancelled three studio commitments in the past four months. Her professional reputation, carefully built over a decade, has begun to fray at the edges in ways she is acutely aware of but feels unable to address.

At home, her partner of six years has described her as "somewhere else," and Renata does not dispute this. She has found herself cycling through periods of flat withdrawal and sudden, disproportionate anger — sharp outbursts over small disruptions that leave her ashamed and her partner confused. Her concentration, once precise enough to hold complex chord arrangements in working memory through a full session, now fractures unpredictably. She has come to believe, with a quiet but settled conviction, that the person she was before the attack — the one who belonged to the world of music, of performance, of easy presence in a crowd — no longer exists in any recoverable form. She had come to feel that the festival did not merely happen to her but revealed something true: that people, even in joyful public spaces, are not what they present themselves to be, and that safety is a story told to those who have not yet learned otherwise. She has no clear picture of her future. When she tries to imagine herself at fifty, the image does not form.

What finally brought Renata to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which she walked out of a recording booth mid-take, sat in her car for two hours, and drove home without telling anyone why. She told the therapist she was not sure she wanted to recover so much as she wanted to understand whether recovery was something that still applied to her.
